1 big thing: The terrifying rise of AI hacking tools
By Sam Sabin
 

Illustration: Gabriella Turrisi/Axios
 

A new breed of widely available AI tools is helping hackers launch cyberattacks around the clock, breaching corporate networks in a matter of hours and overwhelming defenders.

Why it matters: AI-enabled hacking is still in its infancy, but open-source tools — which are free to download — are fundamentally changing the economics of cybercrime.

  • Hackers can launch self-adjusting attack plans allowing agents to find vulnerabilities and steal credentials, sometimes before human defenders realize their systems are being probed.

Driving the news: Recent cyberattacks involving publicly available "AI agent frameworks" are drawing warnings about how quickly hackers can infiltrate corporate networks.

  • The FBI warned Friday that hackers have used an AI framework called Artex to attack organizations worldwide, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.
  • In a separate report Friday, Amazon said hackers used Artex to steal AI model credentials, then used those stolen resources to power additional attacks.
  • Last week, developer platform Railway and blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack also reported attacks involving Artex.
  • Palo Alto Networks said Thursday that Chinese-speaking hackers used another open-source framework, Cairn, to conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations between August and September. In a separate report Monday, Google said hackers used Cairn during an intrusion into the U.S. aerospace sector.
  • CrowdStrike also saw one group using Artex to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over 11 days week last month.

Reality check: Cyberattacks are still scary, and tech resiliency is still built on a faulty internet foundation, making mishaps possible even without clear evidence of AI-assisted hacks.

  • A litany of popular services — including Microsoft, Apple, Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviations Administration and the National Security Agency — have all reported outages in the last week.
  • An unknown group infected about 178 major websites with crypto-stealing malware through the Optimizely Web Experimentation platform in less than a day, according to Report URI. Affected websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab and Ikea, and AI doesn't seem to be involved as of now.

What they're saying: "We're seeing more active attacks than ever right now," Sam Rubin, senior vice president of Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 threat intelligence and consulting unit, told Axios.

How it works: Artex and Cairn use AI agents to automate tasks hackers traditionally performed themselves.

  • A hacker gives the framework a target and an objective, such as breaking into a company's network.
  • AI agents develop attack plans, search for vulnerabilities and use hacking tools to test possible entry points.
  • The agents share findings and adjust tactics when something fails, allowing them to operate around the clock without constant human supervision.

2. Nvidia says it'll be "selective" with capital
By Ina Fried
 

Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

Nvidia's interim CEO said yesterday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward.

Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital.

What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said at the end of a conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this."

  • She said the company would continue to use its balance sheet and support startups and the broader AI ecosystem, but she made clear it won't be a blank check.

Catch up quick: The company posted stronger-than expected sales of $116 billion, a reminder of how formidable its business remains even after Jensen Huang resigned last week.

  • The company's shares rose by as much as 5% in after-hours trading, and the stock prices of Coreweave and Nebius, so-called neoclouds that Nvidia has backstopped in the past, each rose by more than 10%.

3. Microsoft debuts six AI models
By Ina Fried
 

Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Penguin Random House
 

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells Axios the software giant is making significant progress toward building its own frontier general-purpose AI model, even as it introduces six specialized models that it claims rival leading offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic at a fraction of the cost.

Why it matters: Microsoft has long relied on OpenAI and other AI companies for its most advanced models. Now it's demonstrating that it can develop competitive technology of its own, and the new offerings show how aggressively the tech giant plans to compete on price.

Driving the news: Microsoft announced six new AI models yesterday at its Ignite conference in San Francisco. The models span coding, cybersecurity, image generation and voice.

  • MAI Code 2: Microsoft says its new coding model delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the price and 96% of Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5's performance at just 5% of the cost.
  • MAI Code 2 Flash: A smaller, faster model that Microsoft says matches GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the cost.
  • MAI Cyber 2 Flash: A cybersecurity model that Microsoft says beats GPT-6 Astra on a security benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task.

Between the lines: Microsoft's strategy is to build models specialized for particular tasks, allowing them to achieve comparable performance at significantly lower costs.

  • "It basically means that you cram more tokens and knowledge and expertise into the same amount of parameters," Suleyman tells Axios.
  • The trade-off is that a model optimized for everyday coding tasks won't be as capable at advanced math or scientific research.
  • Microsoft's performance comparisons rely on selected benchmarks, and some pricing advantages reflect promotional discounts.

The big picture: Even as Microsoft targets the industry's leaders, frontier AI keeps moving forward. OpenAI yesterday announced GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, with the new Astra priced 20% less than the prior version.
 
 
4. Why Dems want to slow Anthropic's $1T IPO
By Maria Curi
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

A group of elected officials from five states led by Democrats is seeking to pressure Anthropic to square its warnings of catastrophic risk with plans to go public.

Why it matters: The questions for the company aren't likely to stop the IPO, but they are a preview of the scrutiny tech giants can expect to face after the midterms' blue AI earthquake.

  • While Democrats have yet to build a comprehensive AI policy platform, it's already clear that many do not favor acceleration.

Elected officials and fiscal stewards in Maryland, Illinois, Colorado, Connecticut and New Mexico are demanding that Anthropic tackle crucial issues before it starts trading, according to a letter sent to CEO Dario Amodei and the Anthropic board.

  • "Innovation cannot come at the expense of accountability and transparency, especially when the retirements of our teachers, firefighters, police and all state workers are on the line," Maryland State Comptroller Brooke Lierman said in a statement.

The solution the state officials propose is to bake in a sunset of the founders' rights and to disclose "far more" about how Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust would operate given that its trustees elect directors.

5. Training data
 
  • OpenAI debuted the 6.2 versions of its Sol and Astra models, though the new releases got a few poor early reviews. (VentureBeat)
  • Anthropic is expected to price its IPO at the high end or above its range of $70 to $78 per share. (Bloomberg)
 
 
6. + This
 

Upside Foods said yesterday it is significantly expanding commercial availability of its "cultivated" chicken (it prefers that term to "lab-grown"). Upside says it can now produce 1 million pounds of meat per year with no animals killed.

  • I had the chance to try an early version several years back for "Axios on HBO."
  • Spoiler alert: It tastes like chicken.
